verses.translation_literal: And there was a famine in the land, apart from the first famine that was in the days of Abraham; and Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, to Gerar.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hunger came to the land again. Not the first hunger, the old one, the one the family still told of in the days of Abraham, but a second, as if the earth had learned the same cruelty twice. And Isaac rose and went, toward Abimelech, king of the Philistines, toward the walls of Gerar.
verses.directors_commentary: The chapter opens by looking backward: 'apart from the first famine' ties Isaac's story to his father's, and the audience is meant to hear the echo of Genesis 12, where hunger sent Abraham down to Egypt. Ramban says the first famine was remembered and retold, because it was on its account that Abraham went down to Egypt and was greatly honoured there; so Isaac wanted to follow his fathers' road. Isaac stands at the same fork. Canaan lives on the winter rains, not on a river, so a failed season is real danger for a herding household, and Egypt, watered by the Nile, was the traditional escape (Radak on 26:2). Isaac goes first to Gerar, on the edge of the Philistine coastal plain, to a king with whom his father had made a treaty (Radak on 26:1, citing Genesis 21:23). The commentators split on why. Rashbam reads Gerar as the first stage of a journey meant to end in Egypt, since the road to Egypt ran through Philistine country, which is why God must forbid it in the next verse. Ramban reads it differently: Isaac went to his father's ally hoping the king would support him through the drought so that he would not need to go down to Egypt at all. Sforno has him going to ask the king's leave before leaving the land. The KJV 'beside' is archaic for 'apart from, in addition to', and 'unto Gerar' flattens the Hebrew directional ending -ah ('toward Gerar'). The reader should not picture the later Iron Age enemies of Samson and David when the text says 'Philistines': here they are a settled coastal people ruled by a king who honours an old treaty.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'from alone, separate from': this famine is set apart from the earlier one and counted in addition to it. The KJV 'beside' means 'in addition to' here, not 'next to'.

'My father is king' (or 'father of a king'). Radak on 26:9 says Philistine kings were commonly called Abimelech, as Egyptian kings were called Pharaoh; Ramban on 26:1 leaves open whether this is Abraham's contemporary.
Gerar with the directional ending -ah: 'toward Gerar'. The journey, not only the destination, is in the word.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH appeared to him and said, "Do not go down [to] Egypt; dwell in the land that I will say to you."
verses.translation_dramatic: And the LORD appeared to him, and spoke: "Do not go down to Egypt. Stay. Dwell in the land that I will show you."
verses.directors_commentary: The command is a prohibition first: 'do not go down'. 'Down' is geographic and literal: Egypt lies downhill and to the south of the hill country, and the verb is the one used of Abraham's descent in Genesis 12. Rashi says Isaac was already planning the trip, as his father had done in the famine, and is told that he is a perfect offering and that no land outside this one is fit for him; Radak adds that Egypt was well fed because the river waters it, and that the land of the Philistines was less hungry than the rest of Canaan, so Isaac is better off staying; Sforno ties the prohibition to the shortage of pasture that would have pushed him out. The final clause is deliberately open: 'the land that I will say to you' is the formula of Genesis 22:2, 'one of the mountains that I will say to you'. God does not name the destination; Isaac must trust the next instruction. Ramban reads it as guidance for his whole life: wherever God tells him, there he is to settle, and for now, in Gerar. Radak notes that the verse says 'dwell' (shekhon) and the next says 'sojourn' (gur), to press the command that he not leave the land, now or ever. The KJV 'tell thee of' adds a preposition the Hebrew does not have; the Hebrew has God as the speaker of the place. YLT's 'tabernacle' is over-literal for shekhon, which means 'settle, take up residence' and is the root of Shekhinah, 'dwelling presence'.

philological_notes.note: 'Go down', with the directional -ah on Egypt (mitzrayemah). The geography is part of the sense: Egypt is the lowland, and the verb recalls Abraham's descent.
'Settle, tent, dwell'. Not a transient stay; it is the verb of semi-permanent pastoral residence. Radak distinguishes it from the 'sojourn' (gur) of the next verse.
'That I will say to you': the destination is not named. The same wording introduces the mountain in Genesis 22:2. Ramban reads it as guidance given from time to time.

verses.translation_literal: Sojourn in this land, and I will be with you, and I will bless you; for to you and to your seed I will give all these lands, and I will establish the oath that I swore to Abraham your father.
verses.translation_dramatic: Live as a stranger in this land, and I will be with you. I will bless you. To you, and to your children after you, I will give all these lands, and I will make good the oath I swore to Abraham, your father.
verses.directors_commentary: The command softens from 'dwell' to 'sojourn' (gur): Isaac is a resident alien, with no title to the land, and the promise is therefore a gift not yet possessed. The sequence is the heart of it: presence ('I will be with you'), blessing, then land. The three verbs are all first person future; God does the work and Isaac only has to stay. The promise is stated as the fulfilment of an oath, which here has a legal force: a sworn oath binds the swearer. Ramban notes this verse is the only oath recorded for Isaac, and later biblical language ('the land I swore to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob') treats it as his. 'These lands' is plural: not one territory but the whole mosaic of Canaanite and Philistine peoples (Ramban on Genesis 26:2, Radak on 26:4). Rashi's one remark is philological: ha'el is an old form of ha'elleh, 'these', as the Targum confirms. The KJV renders 'countries', which suggests nation-states; 'lands' is closer. The KJV 'perform' for 'establish' loses the verb hakimoti, 'I will cause to stand', a word of legal confirmation.

philological_notes.note: 'Live as a resident alien, sojourn': a person with protection but not with ownership. It heads the verse and contrasts with 'give' later in it.
A rare, older form of 'these' (usually ha'elleh).
Causative of 'stand': 'I will cause to stand, confirm'. Used for the validation of an oath or covenant.

verses.translation_literal: And I will multiply your seed like the stars of the heavens, and I will give to your seed all these lands, and all the nations of the earth will bless themselves by your seed.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will make your children countless as the stars of heaven. I will give your children all these lands. And in your children every nation on earth will find the words of its blessing.
verses.directors_commentary: Three promises, as the opening is repeated and expanded: descendants, land, and a blessing that reaches beyond the family. The star image is nighttime desert imagery, and for a man whose father also counted stars (Genesis 15) it is a family inheritance. The last clause uses the reflexive stem hitbarechu, 'they will bless themselves'. The KJV 'shall be blessed' reads it as a passive and makes Isaac's line the channel of blessing; the Hebrew form more naturally means that the nations will use his descendants as the pattern in their own blessings, as Rashi explains: a person will say to his son, 'May your seed be like the seed of Isaac' (Rashi on Genesis 26:4, comparing the formula of Genesis 48:20, and of curses and oaths). BBE's 'will be a blessing' is a third reading, and is why this phrase is argued over. Radak narrows 'seed' to Jacob's line. The literal layer keeps 'seed' because the Hebrew is a collective singular, and 'seed' is the agrarian image that the harvest of verse 12 will pick up.

philological_notes.note: Reflexive/middle stem: 'bless themselves, invoke blessing by'. Not simply passive. Rashi explains it as nations using Isaac's offspring as the model in their blessings.
'Seed', singular collective for offspring. It anticipates the verb zara' ('he sowed') in verse 12.

verses.translation_literal: Because that Abraham listened to my voice, and he kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my instructions.
verses.translation_dramatic: All this, because Abraham listened to my voice. He kept my charge. He kept my commandments, my statutes, my teachings.
verses.directors_commentary: The reason clause is the theology of the whole promise: it rests on obedience, and the word is 'listened' (shama'), which in Hebrew is both hearing and heeding. 'Ekev, 'heel, consequence', is the same word as in Genesis 22:18, and Rashbam ties the clause to the binding of Isaac. For an audience that knows that story, the irony is sharp: the listener Isaac is told his father's obedience is his security. The four terms that follow are a string of legal vocabulary. The KJV gives them as five clauses of equivalent weight, but the Hebrew piles them up to mean 'everything he was bidden' (Ibn Ezra on 26:5). Rashi and Ramban unpack them into later categories (rabbinic fences, rational laws, irrational decrees, oral Torah), and Rashbam reads them more modestly as the customs of the age before Sinai. The text does not say that Abraham knew the Mosaic law; it uses the technical vocabulary of royal covenant to say that he was a model vassal. KJV 'charge' for mishmeret is fair, meaning 'what is to be guarded', as the verb 'kept' (shamar) makes plain by sound: shama'... vayishmor, 'he listened... and he guarded'.

philological_notes.note: From 'heel': 'as a consequence of, because'. The same idiom is used of Abraham in Genesis 22:18.
Two verbs of near-identical sound: 'listened' and 'kept'. The pairing is the point: obedience as hearing and then guarding.

A legal list. Ibn Ezra reads it as a summary of all that Abraham was bound to keep, perhaps the commands 'go forth' and 'take your son'. Rashi, Ramban and Radak read each term as a distinct class of later law.

verses.translation_literal: And Isaac dwelt in Gerar.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Isaac stayed. He settled in Gerar, as he had been told.
verses.directors_commentary: A short, obedient sentence that does a lot of work. The verb is yashav, 'sat down, settled', and the narrator gives no hesitation. Ibn Ezra and Radak say simply that he did what God had commanded. Note what it leaves unsaid: God's word had been 'dwell in the land that I will say', and Isaac settles in Gerar on his own reading of that. The KJV 'dwelt' is exact. Notice also that he is settling in a city-state's territory as a resident alien without land rights, so his safety rests on the goodwill of the king and the people, which is the setup for the next verse.

verses.translation_literal: And the men of the place asked about his wife, and he said, "She is my sister," for he was afraid to say, "My wife," lest the men of the place kill me because of Rebekah, for she was good of appearance.
verses.translation_dramatic: The men of the place began to ask about his wife. "She is my sister," Isaac said. He was afraid to say "my wife." The men of this place might kill him for Rebekah, because she was beautiful to look at.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the third time the family tells this lie (Genesis 12 and 20 are the other two), and the audience should hear it as a family reflex. The fear is a legal-social calculation: in a world with no one to protect a foreign herdsman, a husband stands between a beautiful woman and a king's household, and the easiest way to take her is to remove him. A sister, by contrast, can be negotiated for, so brotherly protection is a bargaining position, not a safety. Note the pivot: the men 'asked about his wife' (the preposition le-ishto means 'concerning'; Rashi and Radak read it as 'about his wife' and compare Genesis 20:13). The KJV's 'asked him of his wife' is accurate but archaic. The narrator gives Isaac's thought in free indirect speech, 'he was afraid to say', and then uses the plain phrase tovat mar'eh, 'good of appearance'. Ramban adds a small realistic detail: they asked about the wife, not the children, so Isaac could say that the children came from another woman. 'Kill me' is hrg, murder, not execution.

philological_notes.note: 'Concerning his wife', not 'asked his wife'. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak all explain the le- as 'about, on account of'.
'Good of appearance': an idiom for physical beauty, the same phrase used of Sarah's beauty in the earlier stories.

verses.translation_literal: And it was, when the days grew long for him there, that Abimelech, king of the Philistines, looked down through the window, and he saw, and behold: Isaac [was] playing with Rebekah his wife.
verses.translation_dramatic: The days went on, and on, and the lie settled into habit. Then one day Abimelech, king of the Philistines, looked down from his window and saw. And there was Isaac, laughing with Rebekah, as a man laughs with his wife.
verses.directors_commentary: The scene turns on a pun. The Hebrew says 'Yitzchak metzachek', 'Isaac was isaac-ing': the verb tzachak is the root of his own name ("he laughs"). The KJV's 'sporting' and the modern 'playing' are fine, but they lose the sound; a literal reader should hear the name echo. The verb is also used of intimate play: Rashi says Abimelech saw him 'in the act of marriage', and Rashbam compares the use of the same verb in Genesis 39:17 (Potiphar's wife's accusation), where it is sexual. The dramatic layer keeps to what is visible: the intimacy of a husband and wife, which no brother and sister would share. Rashi and Rashbam both note the time clause: with the long days Isaac stopped being careful, because nothing had happened to him. The king looks 'down' (hishqif, a bending look) 'through the window', a detail that is plain scene-setting: the palace overlooks the courtyards, and the king can watch unseen. A king observing a guest from above is also a picture of power.

philological_notes.note: 'Laughing, playing, making love'. The verb of Isaac's own name (yitzchak), so the text calls him 'Isaac-ing'. In context the playing is marital intimacy, as Rashi and Rashbam read it.
'He looked down, peered'. A downward gaze from a height, used of looking from a window or over a valley.

verses.translation_literal: And Abimelech called Isaac and said, "Surely, behold, she is your wife! And how did you say, 'She is my sister'?" And Isaac said to him, "Because I said, 'Lest I die on account of her.'"
verses.translation_dramatic: Abimelech sent for Isaac. "She is your wife," he said. "Surely, she is your wife! How could you say, 'She is my sister'?" And Isaac answered him, with nothing to hide behind now: "Because I thought, I might die for her."
verses.directors_commentary: The king's logic is the logic of the window: no man plays like that with his sister (Radak on Genesis 26:9). The particle 'ach is emphatic and corrective, 'but surely', and the double exclamation is the king speaking in a tone between indignation and relief. Isaac's answer is the shortest confession in Genesis: he states his fear in the very words of the earlier verse, 'lest I die', and offers no excuse. The KJV's 'of a surety' is archaic for the same emphatic ach; 'lest I die for her' is faithful, though the Hebrew al-eiha means 'on her account' and so carries both 'for her sake' and 'because of her'. Radak argues that this cannot be Abraham's Abimelech, since that king would not have had to ask how Isaac could say it, having been through the same trap with Sarah. The narrator lets the reader decide.

philological_notes.note: A corrective, emphatic particle: 'but surely, in truth'. Radak glosses it 'but' and compares Exodus 31:13 and 21:21.
'Lest I die on her account': both 'for her sake' and 'because of her'. The preposition 'al does the work of the English 'for'.

verses.translation_literal: And Abimelech said, "What is this you have done to us? Within a little, one of the people lay with your wife, and you would have brought guilt upon us."
verses.translation_dramatic: "What have you done to us?" Abimelech said. "One of my people might easily have lain with your wife. It was that close. And you would have brought guilt down on all of us."
verses.directors_commentary: Abimelech's anger is not about the lie itself but about what it nearly cost. The key word is kim'at, 'within a little, almost': this is a near miss, and nothing has happened. Radak puts it plainly: the thing was close. Since Isaac had said she was his sister, no one saw any wrong in approaching her, and the whole community would have borne guilt, 'asham, for it, because Isaac is great and beloved of God. Radak compares Psalm 73:2, 'my feet had almost slipped'. In the world of the story, adultery with another man's wife brings guilt on the whole community, and the injured party has a claim on heaven. This echoes Genesis 20, where Abimelech's household was struck. Ramban adds that the king himself kept his hands off her out of regard for Abraham's covenant, and that this is why he can say the guilt of the earlier episode would have been repeated. The KJV 'might lightly have lien with' is archaic: 'lightly' means 'easily', and 'lien' is an old participle. The verb shakhav is the plain Hebrew 'lie with', and the English should not soften it. 'One of the people' (achad ha'am) is read by Rashi and Sforno as 'the one distinguished among the people', the king himself, who would have taken her without asking; the plain sense is 'any one of the people'. 'Guilt' (asham) is also the name of a later sacrifice, the guilt offering, so the word has a ritual ring.

philological_notes.note: 'Almost, within a little': a near miss, with the verb in the perfect. Radak says the thing was close, and compares Psalm 73:2, 'my feet had almost slipped'.
'One of the people'. Rashi and Sforno read it as 'the unique one among the people', the king; the plain sense is any ordinary man.
'Guilt, liability'. The word later names the guilt offering in the cult. Sforno notes that when the great man of a generation is struck, harm spreads to those who shelter in his shadow.

verses.translation_literal: And Abimelech commanded all the people, saying, "The one touching this man and his wife: dying, he shall be put to death."
verses.translation_dramatic: Then Abimelech gave his order to all the people, and he said it plainly: "Whoever touches this man or his wife shall surely die."
verses.directors_commentary: The king turns his fear into law. The formula mot yumat, 'dying he shall be put to death', is the standard emphatic phrase for a capital offence, and the king uses it on his own authority. Note what the verb says: 'touches' (noge'a) is wider than rape or murder; it covers any laying of hands, and it protects both husband and wife. This is the reversal of Isaac's fear: the lie that was meant to protect him ends with the king himself declaring him inviolable. The KJV is accurate. Radak observes that the order protects Isaac as well as Rebekah, since the people's concern had been to remove him. The people receive an order, not an explanation, and the scene closes on law, not on rebuke: Isaac is never reproached by God for the lie, which is itself worth remarking.

philological_notes.note: Infinitive absolute plus passive imperfect: 'he shall surely be put to death'. The formula of capital law.
'The one touching': any physical contact or harm. Radak reads the order as protecting Isaac from being killed, as well as Rebekah from being taken.

token_glosses.gloss: he shall be put to death

verses.translation_literal: And Isaac sowed in that land, and he found in that year a hundred measures, and YHWH blessed him.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Isaac sowed seed in that land, in the year of hunger, in a country not his own. And in that same year he found a hundred measures for every one that was looked for. The LORD had blessed him.
verses.directors_commentary: The sentence is built to astonish by its doubled 'that': 'in that land, in that year'. Rashi and Rashbam both read the repetition as a concession: the land was hard and the year was a year of drought, and still it yielded. Isaac is a herdsman, and sowing grain is itself a surprise, a step from nomad to farmer, on the edge of the Negev, where a good field might return perhaps ten-fold at best. The Hebrew says 'a hundred she'arim', a phrase that has no certain meaning. The ancient commentators read it as 'a hundred times the estimate', since the appraisers had assessed what the field should yield (Rashi, Rashbam, Radak); Ibn Ezra relates the word to the root meaning 'to estimate, to reckon'. The KJV 'an hundredfold' is a reasonable interpretation, but it is an interpretation; the text itself is a puzzle, and the translator should leave it one. The last words give the cause, in the order that matters: the harvest comes first, then the explanation, 'and YHWH blessed him', and the blessing fulfils the promise of verse 3, 'I will be with you and bless you', as Sforno notes.

philological_notes.note: Obscure. Rashi, Rashbam and Radak read it as 'estimates' (from the root of 'reckon'): a hundred times what the appraisers had estimated. Ibn Ezra relates it to Proverbs 23:7. The same consonants also spell 'gates', which is why some readers are puzzled.
'And he found': the harvest is described as a finding, a discovery, not a labour, which suits the theme of unearned blessing.

verses.translation_literal: And the man became great, and went, going and becoming great, until that he became great exceedingly.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the man grew great. He did not grow once and stop; he went on growing, day after day, going and growing, until the greatness of him was beyond all measure.
verses.directors_commentary: The Hebrew builds a staircase out of one root: gadal, 'he became great', then 'he went on going and becoming great' (halokh we-gadel), then gadal again at the top. Every rung is the same word, so the reader feels the wealth compounding. The KJV 'waxed great, and went forward, and grew' uses three different English verbs and loses the single root; the literal layer keeps 'great' four times. Note that 'great' here means rich and powerful, not tall or old: this is the language of status. The idiom hālōkh we-gādēl (a continuous infinitive plus a participle or adjective) is the Hebrew way of saying 'steadily more and more', and the ASV 'more and more' catches the sense if not the sound. Play the scene as slow accumulation, not a windfall; the previous verse gave a hundredfold harvest in a famine year, and in a world where famine is the norm, steady surplus is what makes a man dangerous to his neighbours. Rashi (citing Genesis Rabbah) says people proverbially said 'the dung of Isaac's mules, not the silver and gold of Abimelech', that is, even the leavings of Isaac's animals were worth more than the king's treasury.

philological_notes.note: An infinitive absolute of 'go' joined to an adjective or participle of 'grow' expresses ongoing, steady increase: 'going and growing'. Radak reads halokh as an infinitive and gadel as an adjective or infinitive, comparing 'bashel mevushal' in Exodus 12:9.
The verb opens and closes the verse and the middle word shares its root: greatness in wealth and standing, which Radak glosses as riches and possessions.

verses.translation_literal: And there was to him a possession of flock and a possession of herd and a great workforce; and the Philistines were jealous of him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Flocks were his, and herds, and a vast company of hands to tend and till and drive them. And the Philistines looked on, and the looking soured into envy.
verses.directors_commentary: Wealth in this world is not coin but animals and the people who work them. Mikneh, 'possession', is movable property, livestock above all; 'avuddah is a rare word for the labour force itself, which is why the commentators split: Rashi takes it as 'a great deal of activity', Ibn Ezra as servants and maidservants, Rashbam and Radak as fieldwork, since without further qualification 'avodah means work on the soil. The KJV 'great store of servants' and ASV 'great household' choose one reading and hide that the Hebrew is deliberately broad: Isaac has hands, fields and flocks all at once. Then the turn: vayqan'u, 'they were jealous', is the same root as zealous, hot, covetous passion, not mild 'envy' as KJV and ASV have it. The jealousy is a political fact: in a city-state economy a foreign guest richer than the locals threatens the king's standing, and Ramban notes that this wealth was in livestock and labour, not silver and gold as with Abraham. Sforno adds that the Philistines' own fields were failing at the time they saw his success. Expect that sourness to turn practical in the next verse.

philological_notes.note: A rare collective noun built on the root 'to work/serve': workforce, the sum of labour. Commentators dispute whether it means servants, agricultural work, or generally 'much doing'.
'They were jealous / zealous against', the verb used elsewhere of God's jealousy. It is stronger than idle envy: it is the heat of rivalry that leads to action.

verses.translation_literal: And all the wells that the servants of his father had dug in the days of Abraham his father, [the] Philistines stopped them up and filled them [with] earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: As for the wells, every one that his father's servants had dug in Abraham's day, the Philistines had stopped them, choked them, and heaped them full of earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
Water is wealth in the Negev border country, and a well is a title deed: whoever digs it and holds it owns the pasture around it. That is why the Philistines do not merely ignore these shafts; they destroy them. Rashi hears a defensive motive (the wells would be a stumbling-block, drawing hostile armies), Radak a fear that Isaac's strength would one day grow like his father's, and Sforno envy. In a land that lives by rainfall and a few deep shafts, filling a well with earth is an act of war without a weapon.

The grammar matters. The object comes first, 'and all the wells ... the Philistines stopped them', which marks background: this had happened already, so the KJV's 'had stopped' is a fair reading, not a mistake, and so is the ASV's. The verb is satam (s-t-m), 'to stop up', and the narrator will return to it in verse 18 with the same root, 'they had stopped them after Abraham died', which tells us the damage dates to the time of Abraham's death, not to Isaac's rise. The KJV's 'earth' is right; 'afar is loose soil, dust, the stuff of a heap.

philological_notes.note: 'They stopped them up': the verb satam, to block or shut, with a pronoun suffix. The root recurs in 26:18, tying the two verses together. Rashi explains the motive and renders it with an Aramaic word for hiding or blocking.
Dust, loose earth. The wells are not merely closed but packed solid, so that digging them again means clearing, not just uncovering.

verses.translation_literal: And Abimelech said to Isaac, Go from with us, for you have become too mighty from us exceedingly.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Abimelech spoke to Isaac. "Go. Leave us. You have grown too strong for us, far too strong."
verses.directors_commentary: This is the king's whole policy in four words: lekh me'immanu, 'go from with us'. He gives no charge and no crime, only a fact about size. The key word is 'atzamta mimmennu, literally 'you have become mighty from us', a comparative built on min: Isaac has grown out of us, bigger than us. The KJV 'much mightier than we' is acceptable, but it flattens the pun on departure; the same preposition min that means 'than' also means 'from', so the king says 'go from us because you are great from us', as though Isaac has already half-left. Ramban hears a second layer: Abimelech says that even he, the king, has no such livestock and workforce, and it is a disgrace that a guest's house is greater than the royal house. Radak notes the king may also be protecting Isaac, since he had warned his people against touching him; moving away may be safer. Note that earlier in the chapter this same man received Isaac as a guest; the hospitality has flipped, and the man whose wealth is the blessing of God is now politely expelled for it.

philological_notes.note: 'You have become mighty/numerous more than/from us.' The preposition min serves both comparison and separation, giving a quiet pun with 'go from us'.

verses.translation_literal: And Isaac went from there, and encamped in the wadi of Gerar, and dwelt there.
verses.translation_dramatic: So Isaac went. He did not argue. He struck his camp and pitched it again in the wadi of Gerar, and there he settled.
verses.directors_commentary: Three verbs, each plain: he went, he encamped, he dwelt. Isaac does not answer the king; the text records only the movement. The word nachal is a wadi, a seasonal watercourse bed, not a green 'valley' as the KJV and ASV have it; it is where the water table is nearest the surface, which is exactly why a man with flocks would go there. Radak notes that nachal can name a whole low-lying district, even one with a town in it, and Rashi and Ramban both stress that the place is at a distance from the city, so he leaves Gerar but not the territory. The verb vayyichan is the camper's verb, 'he pitched camp', not 'built'; it signals a mobile household with tents. The last verb, vayyeshev, 'and he sat/dwelt', is the first sign of settling. This is Isaac's pattern in the chapter: avoid the fight and relocate. Ramban argues it is the same area, only farther from the city; we should not assume he left Philistine land altogether.

philological_notes.note: A wadi: a watercourse, often dry except in the rains. Radak shows the word can name the low land itself, with a town in it, citing Deuteronomy 2:36 and 2 Samuel 24:5. KJV 'valley' misses the dry-bed sense.

verses.translation_literal: And Isaac returned and dug the wells of water which they had dug in the days of Abraham his father, and the Philistines had stopped them up after the death of Abraham; and he called to them names like the names which his father had called to them.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Isaac turned back to the old work. He dug again the wells of water that had been dug in his father's days, the ones the Philistines had choked after Abraham died. And he gave them back their names, the very names his father had spoken over them.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse is mostly looking backward, and the grammar shows it: 'they had dug', 'they had stopped', 'he had called'. Isaac is not discovering anything; he is re-establishing a claim. The Hebrew vayyashov, 'he returned', and then 'vayyachpor', 'he dug', suggests he went back to reopen the shafts, and the KJV's 'digged again' captures the turn if not the pun on 'return'. The detail the KJV mentions but does not explain is the naming: in the ancient Near East, to name a place is to assert ownership and to publish it. Rashbam says the old names were kept 'so that no one could dispute', and Radak that the names restore the wells to their first title. Reusing Abraham's names is therefore a legal act, a public deed of inheritance. The timing clause 'after the death of Abraham' matters: the Philistines stopped the wells only once the old man, who had a treaty over wells with the king, could no longer enforce it. Note the contrast with verse 15, which gave the same fact from the Philistines' side.

philological_notes.note: 'He called to them names': naming as a claim of ownership. Isaac gives the same names his father had used, re-establishing the first title.
'And he returned', used here with an adverbial sense 'again' (as KJV 'digged again'), but also a literal turning back to the old sites.

verses.translation_literal: And the servants of Isaac dug in the wadi, and found there a well of living water.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Isaac's servants dug down into the wadi, and there, beneath the dry bed, they struck a well of living water, water that moved.
verses.directors_commentary: The phrase mayim chayyim, 'living water', is the ancient term for water that flows, as from a spring, against the still water of a cistern. In an arid land the difference is life or death for a herd; a cistern empties, a spring does not. The KJV 'springing water' interprets the idiom well, but it hides that the Hebrew says literally 'living', a word with weight elsewhere in Scripture, and the BBE 'came to a spring' is closer to paraphrase than translation. Note that the Hebrew says they found a 'well', not 'water': Radak observes that digging uncovered an older shaft with water already welling in it, which fits a landscape where earlier diggers had also worked. Ibn Ezra glosses chayyim as 'always flowing'. Play the moment as a small miracle: after the king's rejection and the buried wells, the first spade that bites in the new place hits the thing every herdsman prays for.

philological_notes.note: 'Living water': flowing or welling water, as opposed to standing water stored in a cistern. Ibn Ezra explains it as water that flows continually.

verses.translation_literal: And the herdsmen of Gerar quarrelled with the herdsmen of Isaac, saying, The water is ours. And he called the name of the well Esek, for they had contended with him.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the herdsmen of Gerar came and quarrelled with Isaac's herdsmen. "The water is ours," they said. So he named the well Esek, Contention, because they had contended with him over it.
verses.directors_commentary: The speech is three words of Hebrew: lanu ha-mayim, 'to us, the water'. The possessive comes first, as in every land dispute: 'ours!' Water rights are the oldest law in a dry country, and the herdsmen on both sides are the ones at the wellhead, not the kings. Then the name. 'Esek' means 'quarrel, dispute', and the reason clause uses the matching verb hit'asseku, 'they contended', so the name explains itself by sound. The KJV renders the verb 'strove' and leaves the name transliterated, so an English reader cannot hear that the well is called by what was done to it. Ibn Ezra says the word is known from old writings but has no other instance in Scripture; Radak notes that rabbinic Hebrew uses 'asaq for litigation, as in 'when a field is sold and claimants appear'. Radak also gives the reason for naming it: so that, whatever Isaac's later strength, the Gerar herdsmen could never claim the well undisputed, since the name itself testifies to the quarrel. The Targum of Pseudo-Jonathan has a tale of the well drying and returning when handed back; the plain text has none of that.

philological_notes.note: 'Contention, dispute'. The reason clause uses the reflexive verb hit'asseku, 'they quarrelled', so the well's name repeats what was done to it. Rashi glosses 'quarrel, litigation'; Ibn Ezra notes the root has no parallel in Scripture.

'To us, the water': a verbless claim of ownership, with the possessive first for emphasis. Radak compares the dispute between Abraham and Abimelech over a well on the border between Gerar and Beersheba.

verses.translation_literal: And they dug another well, and they quarrelled over it also; and he called its name Sitnah.
verses.translation_dramatic: They dug another well, and there, too, the quarrel came. So he named this one Sitnah, Accusation.
verses.directors_commentary: The second name is harder than the first. Sitnah comes from the root s-t-n, the root of the later word satan, 'adversary, accuser'. The first well was named for a quarrel (Esek); the second is named for open opposition. The KJV leaves it as a bare 'Sitnah' with no gloss, so the English reader meets no meaning at all; YLT's 'Hatred' overshoots, since the root is the adversary's accusation, not emotion. Radak reads the name as 'they are a satan to us, for wherever we dig they dispute with us'. Notice the rhythm of the verse: vayyachperu, vayyarivu, vayyiqra', a three-beat chain of dig, dispute, name, the second loop of a cycle we have just seen. The word gam, 'also', is the exhausted sigh in the middle. Ramban's mystical reading, that the three wells foretell three temples, belongs to his later tradition and is not the plain sense.

philological_notes.note: 'Opposition, accusation', from the root of satan, 'adversary'. Radak glosses it as 'they are an adversary to us'.

verses.translation_literal: And he moved on from there and dug another well, and they did not dispute over it; and he called its name Rehoboth, and he said, "For now YHWH has made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land."
verses.translation_dramatic: He pulled up his stakes and went on from there, and dug another well. This time no one came to quarrel over it. He called it Rehoboth, Wide Places, and said, "Now the LORD has made room for us. Now we shall be fruitful in the land."
verses.directors_commentary:
After Esek, 'Contention', and Sitnah, 'Accusation', Isaac names the third well for what he has been denied: space. The sound play is the point. Rehoboth (rechovot) is answered by the verb in his own speech, hirchiv, 'he has made room', both from rachav, 'wide'. The KJV's 'made room for us' keeps the sense but loses the audible echo of the name.

The verb vaya'tek, 'moved on', is the ordinary word for pulling up and shifting camp, here simply leaving the contested ground behind. Radak understands that Isaac moved all his digging away from their border to a place no one could contest, and Rashbam that he went far from their grazing, which is why no one disputed. Notice that the name is a testimony: Isaac does not say he won, he says YHWH has given room. The second clause, 'we shall be fruitful', uses the root of 'be fruitful and multiply': the patriarchal blessing is heard here as a promise about land and flocks. The KJV 'we shall be fruitful' is faithful; the YLT's perfect 'have been fruitful' mistakes the sequence, which is consequence of the room just granted.

philological_notes.note: 'He moved on': the Hiphil of 'atak, to move or shift away. The plain sense is that Isaac relocated his works away from the contested ground to avoid further dispute, not a claim about any ritual or tent-pegging.
'Wide places', 'broad spaces'. Isaac himself explains the name with the verb hirchiv from the same root, and he joins it to the promise of fruitfulness.
'And we shall be fruitful': the root of the blessing 'be fruitful and multiply'. Onkelos renders it 'and we shall increase' (nifush).

verses.translation_literal: And he went up from there [to] Beer-sheba.
verses.translation_dramatic: From there he went up, up to Beersheba.
verses.directors_commentary:
A short verse, but a turning point: the wandering after water ends, and the next verse will show why. The verb is vaya'al, 'he went up', and the KJV's 'went up' is right; BBE's 'went on' loses it. Radak takes it literally: the land of Israel's holding is higher than the land of the Philistines, which is why Scripture says 'went up' of the Philistines coming against Israel (Judges 15:9) and 'let us go down after the Philistines' (1 Samuel 14:36). Beersheba does stand on higher ground than the coastal plain of Gerar, so the verb is also plain geography. Rashbam, from the next verse's 'Fear not', infers that Isaac was frightened of his neighbours. That is an inference, not something this verse says.

For an actor: no speech, no complaint, only a man who has been pushed from one well to another and has now come to the place his father knew.

philological_notes.note: 'And he went up': literal ascent, as Radak reads it, since the land of Israel lies higher than the Philistine plain. He cites Judges 15:9 ('went up') and 1 Samuel 14:36 ('let us go down after the Philistines').

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH appeared to him in that night, and said, I am the God of Abraham your father. Do not be afraid, for I am with you; and I will bless you and I will multiply your seed on account of Abraham my servant.
verses.translation_dramatic: And that same night the LORD appeared to him. "I am the God of Abraham your father," he said. "Do not be afraid. I am with you. I will bless you, and I will make your seed many, for the sake of Abraham my servant."
verses.directors_commentary: After a chapter of famine, expulsion and quarrels, the first thing God says to Isaac is a name, 'I am the God of Abraham your father', then a command, 'do not be afraid', then the reason, 'I am with you'. The fear is not named in the text, but the command implies it: a man pushed from one wadi to the next, with herdsmen hostile behind him, would be afraid. Ramban and Radak both say the speech answers exactly that. The vision comes at night, the hour of fear and the hour of revelation. The KJV 'the same night' rightly catches the Hebrew 'that night' but 'for my servant Abraham's sake' reorders it: the Hebrew is ba'avur Abraham 'avdi, 'on account of Abraham, my servant'. Calling Abraham 'my servant' gives the patriarch the title later given to Moses and David; Radak says it is because he obeyed all that God commanded him. The promise is entirely in the future, 'I will bless, I will multiply', not the perfect tenses YLT gives, and it echoes the blessing language of Genesis 17 and 22. Note that the ground of the promise is Abraham's, not Isaac's: the son inherits a covenant, he does not originate one.

philological_notes.note: 'On account of, for the sake of'. The preposition ties the promise to Abraham's standing; Radak says it is because Abraham obeyed as a servant, while the Targum Pseudo-Jonathan renders it as 'the merit of Abraham'.
'My servant', a title of honour for one who carried out God's commands, used of Moses and David elsewhere.

verses.translation_literal: And he built there an altar, and he called in the name of YHWH, and he pitched there his tent; and there the servants of Isaac dug a well.
verses.translation_dramatic: There he built an altar. He called on the name of the LORD. There he pitched his tent. And there Isaac's servants dug a well.
verses.directors_commentary:
Four plain acts, each tied to 'there' (sham), which the Hebrew repeats three times: altar, calling, tent, well. The order is the message: the altar and the call on YHWH come before the tent, and the tent before the well. Isaac is doing what his father did at this place, as Radak says of the calling, and the altar answers the night vision of the previous verse.

The KJV 'called upon the name of the LORD' is a fair rendering of the idiom, though it can also mean 'proclaimed'; the Hebrew does not report what he said. 'Pitched' is literal too: vayet is 'stretched out', the verb for spreading a tent. Note the shift in subject: the last act is not Isaac's but his servants', the verb vayichru, 'they dug' (karah, a rarer verb than the chafar of the earlier wells). Ibn Ezra glosses it as 'dug'. The well they dig here is the one the next verses will name, and the narrator leaves it unnamed for now. After three wells lost to quarrel, the digging at Beersheba begins without any dispute reported.

philological_notes.note: 'He called in the name of YHWH': the patriarchal act of worship, here beside a fresh altar. The Hebrew says nothing of what was said, and the idiom is read both as invocation and as proclamation.
'And they dug': a different verb from the chafar used in the earlier verses of this passage, but the same sense; Ibn Ezra glosses it simply as 'dug'.

verses.translation_literal: And Abimelech went to him from Gerar, and Ahuzzat his companion, and Phicol, commander of his army.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then dust rose on the road from Gerar. Abimelech was coming to him, the king himself, and with him Ahuzzath, his companion, and Phicol, the commander of his army.
verses.directors_commentary:
The entrance is a delegation, and the order of the names is the choreography: king, his close companion, then the general. A king does not walk out to a camp of foreigners he has just expelled unless something has changed, and the presence of the army commander tells Isaac, and the audience, that the visit is a matter of state. Play it with the weight of men who are not sure of their welcome.

The KJV makes 'Ahuzzath one of his friends', as though the Hebrew said 'a band of his friends' (so Onkelos, and Rashi, who gives that reading and the alternative, but says it is odd to speak of a king's whole company of friends when only one group is named). Most modern readers take Ahuzzat as a man's name, which Radak also holds, noting the Masorah marks it as unique. 'Friend' here, mere'a, is a court title of a sort: the king's companion. Phicol is the same name that stands beside Abimelech in Abraham's day (Gen 21:22); Radak says it is the same man. If the name is a title or family office, both Abimelechs and both Phicols may be dynastic, which is why the text avoids saying 'the same'.

philological_notes.note: Either 'Ahuzzat, his companion' (a personal name with a court title) or 'a band of his companions' (from the root 'chz, to grasp, hold together). The vowels of ahuzzat show it is a form that would not normally stand alone, so Rashi cites other such forms (ezrat, shekurat). The title 'rea' of the king appears also in 1 Kings 4:5.

verses.translation_literal: And Isaac said to them, Why have you come to me, and you, you hated me, and you sent me away from with you?
verses.translation_dramatic: "Why have you come to me?" Isaac said. "You hated me. You sent me away from you."
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the first time in the chapter Isaac speaks sharply, and the sharpness is all in the grammar: three short clauses strung on 'and', come, hate, send away, with no softening between them. The Hebrew 've'atem', 'and you', puts weight on the pronoun: you, of all people. Play it as a man who has been wronged and who is not yet sure that he is safe.

The background is verse 16 of this chapter, where Abimelech himself told him, 'Go from us, for you have become much mightier than we' (Radak cites the verse and adds that the king had spoken on the advice of his officers). The KJV's 'seeing ye hate me' turns the second clause into a subordinate one, which is defensible, but it hides the plain sequence of the Hebrew. 'Wherefore' is only an archaism for 'why'. The verb 'shilach' in the piel is the word for dismissing, whether a wife, a slave or a guest; on my reading Isaac uses the very word that names what was done to him. The final 'me'itekhem', 'from with you', is a strong preposition of separation: not only 'from you' but out of your company.

philological_notes.note: 'And you sent me away'. The piel of shalach is the verb of dismissal and expulsion (compare Gen 3:23, of Eden); here it names Abimelech's order in verse 16.

verses.translation_literal: And they said, Seeing, we have seen that YHWH has been with you; and we said, Let there be, please, an oath between us, between us and you, and let us cut a covenant with you:
verses.translation_dramatic: "We have seen it," they said, "we have seen it with our own eyes: the LORD is with you. And so we said, let there be an oath between us, between us and you, and let us cut a covenant with you."
verses.directors_commentary:
The delegation answers the accusation by not taking it up, which is how a party that needs something negotiates. The Hebrew doubles the verb, 'ra'o ra'inu', 'seeing, we have seen': an emphatic repetition (the infinitive absolute, here in a rare spelling with vav, as Radak notes, compare Isaiah 6:9), and the KJV's 'we saw certainly' captures the emphasis but loses the repetition. They say 'YHWH', not 'God', the personal name of Isaac's God on foreign lips. Sforno adds that they were not offering a covenant out of fear of Isaac.

The oath is called 'alah', a word that carries a curse as well as a promise, and 'between us' is stuttered three ways: 'beinotenu', 'beininu', 'u-veinekha'. Ibn Ezra explains the first as 'plural upon plural'; Rashi and Rashbam say the oath is the one already between their fathers, to be renewed. Play the repetition as nerves. 'Cut a covenant' is the literal idiom, 'karat berit', from the slaughter of an animal in the ritual; the KJV's 'make' flattens it, and the BBE's 'agreement' flattens it more.

philological_notes.note: Infinitive absolute plus finite verb: 'seeing, we have seen'. The infinitive is spelled with vav in place of the final he, as in Isaiah 6:9 and 30:19, which Radak lists with this.

An oath that carries a curse on whoever breaks it. Ramban compares Deuteronomy 29:11, 'the covenant of the LORD your God and his oath (alah)', and reads the alah here as a sworn curse on whoever breaks the treaty. It is not the usual word for an oath, shevu'ah, which appears in verse 31 as a verb.
'Let us cut a covenant': the idiom is literally 'cut', after the rite of cutting animals in two to seal an agreement. The cohortative ('let us') makes it a proposal, not a done deal.

verses.translation_literal: If you do with us harm, just as we have not touched you, and just as we have done with you only good, and sent you away in peace — you, now, [are] blessed of YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: "Swear that you will do us no harm," they said, "as we never laid a hand on you. We did you nothing but good, and we sent you away in peace. Now you, you are the blessed of the LORD."
verses.directors_commentary:
The terms of the treaty are spoken as a sentence that breaks off. 'If you do us harm...' is the opening of the old oath formula, in which the speaker leaves the curse unspoken because it is too dangerous to say aloud; the KJV smooths it to 'that thou wilt do us no hurt', which is the sense but not the grammar. The actors should leave the ending of the sentence hanging in the air.

What follows is a self-justifying account: 'we did not touch you', 'only good', 'in peace'. It is, to say the least, selective, since they had told him to leave and had stopped up his wells (the story of vv. 15-22). Radak reads the speech charitably, as a reminder that they spared him and sent him off with honour; Ramban reads it as a diplomatic excuse and a hedge, since the Philistines feared Isaac's growing power and Abraham's old treaty (Gen 21:23). 'Touched' (naga') has the sense of laying a hand to harm, as in Gen 26:11. The closing clause is blunt flattery with an edge: 'you, now, blessed of YHWH' means 'you are in a position to hurt us, and we know it' (Radak: God makes you succeed, you could do us harm if you wished). The KJV's 'the blessed of the Lord' adds a definite article the Hebrew does not have.

philological_notes.note: The elliptical oath formula 'if you do ...' with the curse omitted. Read as an oath, it means 'you will not do us harm'.
'Blessed of YHWH'. The passive participle in construct: blessed by him, in his keeping. The speakers acknowledge the divine favour they saw in v. 28.

verses.translation_literal: And he made for them a feast, and they ate and they drank.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Isaac set a feast before them, and the tension went out of the tent. They ate and they drank.
verses.directors_commentary: Five Hebrew words, and the whole chapter pivots on them. Isaac does not answer the speech at all; he answers with food. In the ancient Near East, a covenant is sealed at a table: to eat the same bread is to be bound. The word for feast, 'mishteh', is built on the root 'to drink', so the ceremony is named for the drinking. Radak says the feast was held 'to confirm the love'. The KJV's 'they did eat and drink' is archaic but accurate. The plain sequence, he made, they ate, they drank, gives the actors a pause: nothing is said, and everything is settled.

philological_notes.note: 'Feast, banquet', literally 'drinking'. Covenant meals are a regular feature of treaty-making in Genesis (compare Gen 31:54).

verses.translation_literal: And they rose early in the morning, and they swore, a man to his brother; and Isaac sent them away, and they went from with him in peace.
verses.translation_dramatic: In the early morning they rose, and each man swore to his brother. Then Isaac sent them on their way, and they went from him in peace.
verses.directors_commentary:
The oath is sworn at first light, before the heat and the day's work. 'A man to his brother' is the idiom for mutual obligation, so the oath binds both sides alike, king and nomad. The verb 'vayishave'u', 'they swore', is from the root sh-b-', which is also the root of 'seven'; keep it in your ear, because verse 33 will name the well from it. The KJV's 'betimes' is an archaism for 'early'.

The repetition of 'shalom' deserves attention. 'In peace' echoes verse 29: they said they had sent him away in peace, and now Isaac makes it true by sending them off in peace. The same verb, 'shilach', that began the quarrel at verse 27 ends it. Radak says Isaac accompanied them for a stretch of the road, a courtesy owed to departing guests. Targum Pseudo-Jonathan adds details that are not in the Hebrew: Isaac cuts the bridle of his donkey and gives them a piece as a witness, and he prays for them.

philological_notes.note: 'They swore': the niphal of sh-b-', 'to swear'. The root is the same as that of 'seven', and the usual explanation is that one swore by seven, or bound oneself by seven. It is also the root of Beersheba (v. 33). The wordplay is the point of the sequence.
'He sent them off': the same piel as in vv. 27 and 29. Radak takes it as an escort, 'a measure of accompanying'.

verses.translation_literal: And it was on that day, and the servants of Isaac came, and they told him on account of the well which they had dug, and they said to him, We have found water.
verses.translation_dramatic: That same day Isaac's servants came running to him. They told him about the well they had been digging, and they said, "We have found water."
verses.directors_commentary:
The timing is the point: on that very day, hours after the oath, the well comes in. The text does not say it was a reward, but it lets the audience feel that it was. Radak calls it 'a cause from God' so that the Philistines would see his success and fear him. Ramban sees in it the well of verse 25, which the servants had begun when Abimelech arrived. Play the arrival as news breaking in on a settled moment.

The KJV 'told him concerning the well' renders 'al odot' fairly; the word 'odot' is rare and means 'matters, causes', as in 'on account of'. The servants say 'we have found water' (matsa'nu mayim): in a dry land water is not 'dug', it is 'found'. Notice also that this verse uses 'chafar' for digging where verse 25 used 'kara': two verbs for one act, which the English cannot show. The BBE's 'we have come to water' is a loose paraphrase.

philological_notes.note: A fixed prepositional phrase: 'on account of, concerning'. Related to 'ud', a brand or torch, hence 'the causes, the matter in hand'.
'We have found water'. The standard word for striking water, as in Gen 26:19, where Isaac's servants 'found' a well of living water.

verses.translation_literal: And he called it Shibah; therefore the name of the city is Beer-sheba until this day.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he called the well Shibah. That is why the city is called Beersheba to this very day.
verses.directors_commentary:
Isaac does what his father did and names the place from the oath. The name 'Shiv'ah' is the feminine form of 'seven' and sounds like 'oath' (shevu'ah), so one name carries both the oath sworn in verse 31 and the number. The KJV's 'Shebah' obscures the sound; 'Shibah' is nearer the Hebrew. The verse ends with the narrator's formula 'until this day', a signal that the story was written down when the town was still known by this name.

The commentators disagree about the relation to Abraham's Beersheba (Gen 21:31). Radak says the place was named by both, once for the oath and once more fixed by the repetition; Sforno notes the vowel difference, 'Be'er Sheva' here against 'Be'er Shava' for Abraham, and counts seven wells; Rashbam and Ibn Ezra raise the possibility of two places. The text itself says only 'the city'. Beersheba is the southern limit of the later land, the 'from Dan to Beersheba' of the Bible.

philological_notes.note: 'Seven' and 'oath' share the same root, so 'well of the oath' and 'well of seven' are both heard in the name. Sforno distinguishes the vowels: the 'e' of Sheva' points to both oath and number, the 'a' of Shava' to the oath alone.

verses.translation_literal: And Esau was a son of forty years, and he took a wife, Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath daughter of Elon the Hittite.
verses.translation_dramatic: Esau was forty years old when he took wives: Judith, the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath, the daughter of Elon the Hittite.
verses.directors_commentary:
The scene changes with no transition, and the tone with it. After a chapter of oaths and wells, the narrator drops this in as a flat statement. Forty is Isaac's age when he married Rebekah (25:20), and Radak says Esau waited until he was forty 'as his father did', to look like him; Rashi's reading is far darker, and a rabbinic one. The Hebrew says that Esau 'took a wife', singular, and then names two: the verb serves both, and the text does not say whether they were married together. Notice who is missing: no one chose them for him. Isaac sent a servant for Rebekah; Esau chooses for himself, and Radak contrasts him with Jacob, who would not marry without his parents' consent.

'Hittite' means a people of Canaan, descendants of Heth (Gen 10:15), not the Anatolian empire; they are the local population among whom Abraham bought a burial plot. The KJV's 'took to wife' is idiomatic and fine. Ibn Ezra says Basemath is Adah, that is, one woman with two names, a thing the Bible does many times.

philological_notes.note: 'A son of forty years': the Hebrew idiom for age, 'son of N years'. The KJV 'forty years old' is a fair equivalent.
'The Hittite', from Heth, son of Canaan. Here a local Canaanite people, as in the Machpelah story, not the Anatolian empire.
A woman's name, probably 'fragrance' from the root for spice; Ibn Ezra identifies her with Adah, daughter of Elon.

verses.translation_literal: And they were a bitterness of spirit to Isaac and to Rebekah.
verses.translation_dramatic: And they were a bitterness of spirit to Isaac, and to Rebekah.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Mo'rat ruach', literally 'bitterness of spirit', is not about a family quarrel in the abstract but about two women who made the house a place of conflict for the old couple. The KJV's 'a grief of mind' is gentler than the Hebrew: ruach is breath, wind, spirit, the whole inner person, and 'mo'rat' is the bitter taste of it. The verb 'vatihyena' is feminine plural, which is how the text tells us the grief came from the wives.

The commentators disagree about the root. Rashi takes it from mrh, 'to rebel, defy' (as in 'stubborn and rebellious'); Ibn Ezra prefers mrr, 'bitter' (as in Prov 5:4), and mentions the other view; Radak gives both. Rashi adds, from Genesis Rabbah, that the women practised idolatry, as Targum Pseudo-Jonathan also says; that is rabbinic, not in the Hebrew. The verse also closes the chapter on this shadow, after the oaths and wells, and prepares the next: Rebekah will use this very grief to send Jacob away to find a wife (27:46). Sforno adds that Isaac, grieved though he was, did not see Esau's character, and that this is how he came to stumble over the blessing. That is a later reading, not the text.

philological_notes.note: 'Bitterness of spirit', a construct phrase. The root is disputed: from mrh, 'to rebel, defy' (Rashi), or from mrr, 'to be bitter' (Ibn Ezra). Radak gives both and compares Proverbs 14:10, 'the bitterness of his soul'.

events.title: Famine drives Isaac to Abimelech at Gerar
events.narrative_summary: A famine strikes the land, besides the first one in Abraham's days. Isaac goes to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, at Gerar.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The text gives no date, only that this famine is a second one after the one in Abraham's days (so after Abraham's death, 25:8). I anchor on the end of the birthright sale (25:29-34) with an offset of 5 years and a margin of 15 years, MACRO_ERA. Journey Beersheba-Gerar is 34 km by road, about 1 day by donkey (urim travel); I allow 2 days from Isaac's home in the Negev.
events.ancient_year_marker: In the land a famine, besides the first famine in the days of Abraham

events.title: The LORD forbids Isaac to go to Egypt and renews the promise
events.narrative_summary: The LORD appears to Isaac and tells him not to go down to Egypt but to live in the land he will show him. He promises his presence, blessing, the lands and a numerous seed, because Abraham obeyed.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: No time word. It follows Isaac's arrival at Gerar (26:1), immediately at the END with a 1-month margin. Tier MACRO_ERA, like its scene.

events.title: Isaac tells Gerar's men Rebekah is his sister
events.narrative_summary: Isaac lives in Gerar. When the men of the place ask about his wife, he says she is his sister, afraid they will kill him for her beauty.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows the command to stay (26:2-3, 6) with no stated delay, so it starts at the END of the theophany, margin 1 month; 1 day as the scene of the question and answer. MACRO_ERA.

events.title: Abimelech sees Isaac with Rebekah and protects the couple
events.narrative_summary: After Isaac has been there a long time, Abimelech looks through a window and sees Isaac caressing Rebekah. He rebukes Isaac for the risk of guilt and orders death for anyone who touches the man or his wife.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'When the days were long to him there' (26:8) is a delay without a number: offset 1 year, margin 1 year, from the END of the sister claim. MACRO_ERA. The scene is a single day.
events.ancient_year_marker: When the days were long to him there

events.title: Isaac sows and reaps a hundredfold
events.narrative_summary: Isaac sows in that land and in the same year finds a hundredfold; the LORD blesses him.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'In that year' (26:12): the sowing and the harvest take one agricultural season, about 6 months, placed after the protection decree with no stated gap and a margin of 6 months. SEASONAL_MONTH because it is a growing season. Rashi and Rashbam stress it was a year of famine and drought.

events.title: Isaac grows very rich and the Philistines envy him
events.narrative_summary: Isaac keeps growing until he is very great, with flocks, herds and many servants; the Philistines envy him. They had stopped up with earth all the wells Abraham's servants dug.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'Went on becoming great' (26:13) is a growth over several seasons: duration 2 years, margin 1 year, from the END of the first harvest. The stopping of the wells (26:15) is background, after Abraham's death (26:18). MACRO_ERA.

events.title: Abimelech sends Isaac away and he camps in the wadi of Gerar
events.narrative_summary: Abimelech tells Isaac to leave because he has become much mightier than they. Isaac goes and camps in the wadi of Gerar and lives there.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows the envy with no delay: START at the END of the prosperity, margin 6 months. The move is short (the wadi of Gerar); 1 day. MACRO_ERA.

events.title: Isaac redigs Abraham's wells and the herdsmen quarrel over Esek
events.narrative_summary: Isaac digs again Abraham's wells and gives them his father's names. His servants find a well of living water in the wadi, but Gerar's herdsmen claim it, and he names it Esek.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: No dates. After settling in the wadi, offset 1 month, then 2 months of digging and the quarrel, margin 2 months. Esek is about 5 km from Gerar, 1.5 hours by donkey (urim travel). MACRO_ERA.

events.title: A second well is disputed and called Sitnah
events.narrative_summary: Isaac's servants dig another well and again the herdsmen quarrel over it; he calls it Sitnah.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Sequence 'another well' (26:21): offset 1 month after Esek, duration 1 month, margin 2 months. The text gives no time. MACRO_ERA.

events.title: Isaac digs Rehoboth without dispute
events.narrative_summary: Isaac moves on and digs another well. No one quarrels over it, and he names it Rehoboth, saying the LORD has made room for them to be fruitful in the land.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Sequence 'moved on from there' (26:22): offset 1 month after Sitnah, duration 1 month, margin 2 months. MACRO_ERA.

events.title: Isaac goes up to Beersheba
events.narrative_summary: From there Isaac goes up to Beersheba.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Rehoboth to Beersheba is 35 km straight, about 44 km by road, 11 hours moving, about 1 day by donkey (urim travel). With flocks and a household I allow 2 days. Offset 1 month after Rehoboth, margin 2 months. MACRO_ERA.

events.title: The LORD appears to Isaac at night at Beersheba
events.narrative_summary: That night the LORD appears to Isaac: 'I am the God of Abraham your father. Do not fear, for I am with you. I will bless you and multiply your seed for my servant Abraham's sake.'
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'That night' (26:24, בַּלַּיְלָה הַהוּא) is the night of arrival; the text gives no watch or hour. Midnight is a convention at the centre of the night, with a margin of 6 hours so the window covers the whole night. The Hebrew day begins at sunset, so the night belongs to the day of arrival.

events.title: Isaac builds an altar, pitches his tent and his servants dig a well
events.narrative_summary: Isaac builds an altar there, calls on the name of the LORD and pitches his tent. His servants dig a well there (see the separate digging event).
events.temporal_reasoning_note: After the vision of the night, the altar is built the next morning (BOKER); 26:25 has no time word, so the BOKER placement is a convention. Altar and tent take 3 days, margin 2 days. The digging of the well, which runs on to the day of 26:32, is its own event (evt.gen_26.servants_dig_well) so that the approved covenant event, anchored on this event's END, keeps its dates.

events.title: Isaac's servants dig a well at Beersheba
events.narrative_summary: Isaac's servants dig a well at Beersheba; the work goes on until they strike water (26:32).
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 26:25 gives no time word. The digging begins with the settlement (START of the altar event) and runs until the day water is found (26:32, 'the same day' as the oath). Altar START is day 0 at BOKER; the covenant is altar END (3 days) + 2 weeks, noon of day 17; the oath is the next morning (day 18) and the digging is counted as 18 days, ending at the dawn of the water-day, just before the servants report it (the report is the well_found event, up to midday). Margin 2 days. The BOKER start is a convention, not a time word of 26:25.

events.title: Abimelech, Ahuzzath and Phicol come to Isaac and he feasts them
events.narrative_summary: Abimelech comes from Gerar with Ahuzzath and Phicol. Isaac asks why they come when they hated and expelled him; they answer that they have seen the LORD is with him and ask for an oath and a covenant of non-harm. He makes them a feast and they eat and drink.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: No time word. Gerar to Beersheba is 27 km straight, about 34 km by road, 1 day by donkey (urim travel); the visit begins some weeks after the settlement, offset 2 weeks, margin 2 weeks. I set the arrival at noon (TZOHORAYIM, a convention) and the meal in the evening, 8 hours in all. MACRO_ERA because the delay is vague.

events.title: They rise early, swear to each other and part in peace
events.narrative_summary: The next morning they rise early and swear an oath to each other, and Isaac sends them off, and they leave in peace.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'They rose early in the morning' (26:31): BOKER after the feast. The Hebrew day runs sunset to sunset; the morning is counted as the next calendar morning. Duration 2 hours, margin 1 hour.
events.ancient_diurnal_marker: They rose early in the morning

events.title: Isaac's servants report water and he names the well Shibah
events.narrative_summary: The same day Isaac's servants come and tell him about the well they dug: 'We have found water.' He calls it Shibah, so the city is called Beersheba to this day.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'The same day' (26:32, בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא) has no hour. Window: offset 6 hours from the oath's START with margin 6 hours, covering the daylight of that day. Radak places it before the visitors set out, i.e. inside the oath event; that hour is Radak's reading, not the text's. DAY_SEQUENCE.

events.title: Esau, aged forty, marries two Hittite women
events.narrative_summary: When Esau is forty he takes Judith daughter of Beeri and Basemath daughter of Elon, both Hittites. They are a bitterness of spirit to Isaac and Rebekah.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Esau's age (26:34) is 40 years from the twins' birth (evt.gen_25.twins_born, Isaac aged 60); the same date as Isaac 100 from anchor.isaac_birth. The age covers a whole year: margin 1 year, REGNAL_YEAR. The marriage and the grief are one week. Rashi: Esau waited until 40 to imitate his father.

causal_edges.causal_explanation: The famine sends Isaac toward Egypt as his father once went, and the LORD forbids it and tells him to stay in the land (26:1-2).
Abimelech expels Isaac because he has become much mightier than they (26:16).
The servants' digging at Beersheba ends in finding water, which they report to Isaac (26:25, 32).
Isaac's claim that Rebekah is his sister is what Abimelech discovers, and rebukes, when he sees them together (26:7-9).
Abimelech's party come because they have seen that the LORD is with Isaac (26:28).
The blessed harvest begins the growth in wealth that makes the Philistines envious (26:12-14).
Isaac obeys the command to dwell in the land and so lives in Gerar, where he is asked about his wife (26:2, 6-7).
The LORD's promise 'I will be with you and bless you' (26:3) is followed by the hundredfold harvest and 'the LORD blessed him' (26:12).
After a second quarrel Isaac moves on and digs a well that no one disputes (26:21-22).
Having lost Esek to the quarrel, Isaac's servants dig another well (26:20-21).

The text reuses the name Abimelech for Gerar's king in Abraham's day; whether this is the same man or a royal title is left open.

Daughter of Elon the Hittite, a second wife of Esau taken at forty, and a grief to Isaac and Rebekah. The registry files her under the name Adah, by which Genesis 36 appears to call a Hittite wife of Esau.
A close friend (adviser) of Abimelech who accompanies him to Beersheba to seek a covenant with Isaac.
A Hittite, father of Judith, Esau's wife.
A Hittite, father of Basemath, Esau's wife.
Daughter of Beeri the Hittite. Esau marries her at forty, and she is a grief to Isaac and Rebekah.

systems.name: Covenant feast
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Treaties and covenants were commonly sealed with a shared meal; eating together established friendship and a binding relationship between parties.
rules_and_mechanics: The host prepares a feast for the visiting parties.
Eating and drinking together precedes or accompanies the oath.
The oath is sworn the next morning and the guests depart in peace.

systems.name: Royal edict of protection
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Kings in the ancient Near East could place foreigners or clients under the crown's protection by decree, backed by the death penalty; the guest's safety became a matter of royal honour and the land's guilt.
rules_and_mechanics: The king speaks to all the people publicly.
Anyone who harms or touches the protected person is to be put to death.
The protection covers the person's household, here the wife.

systems.name: Well-digging and water rights
systems.ancient_near_east_context: In the arid Negev, a dug well was a lasting claim on land and pasture. Pastoralists settled disputes over wells by treaty, oath or force, and named wells to record the claim and the event.
rules_and_mechanics: A well dug and used establishes the digger's claim to the water.
Stopping a well with earth voids a rival's claim.
In a dispute the party that yields gives up the well and digs elsewhere; a well no one disputes shows there is room in the land.
The digger names the well, often after the outcome.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Isaac builds an altar at Beersheba.
system_instances.significance_note: He answers the vision with worship, as Abraham did.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Isaac prepares a feast and Abimelech, Ahuzzath and Phicol eat and drink.
system_instances.significance_note: The meal seals the former enemies' reconciliation.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Abimelech orders that anyone who touches Isaac or his wife shall be put to death.
system_instances.significance_note: The foreign king ends up as Isaac's protector, the opposite of Isaac's fear.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Isaac sows in the land and reaps a hundredfold in the same year.
system_instances.significance_note: It shows the LORD's blessing in a famine year and starts the prosperity that provokes Philistine envy.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Isaac calls on the name of the LORD at the altar.
system_instances.significance_note: It marks Beersheba as a worship site of the patriarchs.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The parties rise early, swear to each other and part in peace.
system_instances.significance_note: The oath fulfils the Philistines' request for a non-aggression covenant.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The LORD promises his presence, blessing, the lands, countless seed and blessing of all nations through it.
system_instances.significance_note: Isaac receives the Abrahamic promises in his own right, grounded in Abraham's obedience.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Isaac tells the men of Gerar that Rebekah is his sister, fearing they would kill him for her.
system_instances.significance_note: It repeats the patriarchal wife-sister episodes (Gen 12, 20) and is exposed by Abimelech's window view.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The LORD appears to Isaac at night and tells him not to fear, as he is with him.
system_instances.significance_note: It confirms the promise after the expulsion and before the treaty.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The LORD appears to Isaac and tells him not to go down to Egypt but to dwell in the land he will show him.
system_instances.significance_note: It keeps the promised line in the land during the famine, unlike Abraham's descent to Egypt.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Isaac's servants dig a well beside his tent.
system_instances.significance_note: It sets up the discovery of water in 26:32.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Isaac redigs Abraham's wells and his servants find a living-water well, which the herdsmen of Gerar claim; he names it Esek.
system_instances.significance_note: It ties Isaac to Abraham's claims and starts the pattern of conflict over water.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Isaac digs a third well; nobody quarrels, and he names it Rehoboth.
system_instances.significance_note: He reads the end of the conflict as the LORD making room and promising fruitfulness.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Isaac's servants report water in the new well; he names it Shibah.
system_instances.significance_note: The name explains Beer-sheba and ends the well cycle in peace.

system_instances.outcome_summary: A second well is dug and also disputed; it is named Sitnah.
system_instances.significance_note: Isaac yields again instead of fighting.
